name: California privacy law (CCPA, AB 566, Delete Act)
plain: California rules that let residents opt out of sale and sharing and that require browsers to offer a signal.
meaning: CCPA fines are $2,663 per violation and $7,988 if intentional or involving minors (2025 amounts). AB 566, signed Oct 8 2025, requires browsers to offer an opt out signal from Jan 1 2027. The Delete Act DROP tool opened Jan 2026.

web.api: Legal regime; signals via GPC and cookie settings

access.persistence: Rights apply for the life of the account
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can let California residents opt out of sale and sharing, and require a browser signal
limits.user_action: You click Do Not Sell or Share, or turn on a browser privacy signal
can: Let you opt out of the sale and sharing of your personal data
Let you ask for your data to be deleted, including through the state's deletion tool
Require browsers to offer an opt out signal under AB 566
cannot: Stop all tracking, only the sale and sharing covered by the law
Protect people outside California, unless the company applies it everywhere
Work if the site ignores it, though it can be fined
Delete data that companies must keep for legal reasons

story.what_it_is: California laws that let people opt out of data sale, and push browsers to offer an opt out switch.

marketing.name: CPPA
marketing.pitch: The state privacy agency publishes rules, enforcement news and tools such as the Delete Act request platform for residents.

story.for_you: You may see a Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information link, or a cookie box with a California option. A browser opt out switch, such as Global Privacy Control, can speak for you on every site you visit.
story.for_makers: A site that sells or shares data must honor opt outs, or face fines per violation. Ad companies now add checks for signals like GPC and state laws. Makers also need to keep records and teach teams to turn tags off when a visitor opts out.

use_cases.example: A shopper turns on an opt out signal, and a retailer stops sending the visit to ad networks that would use it for targeting.
A marketing team builds a rule in its tag manager that blocks ad tags for California visitors who opted out.
A game site that sells player data to advertisers must give California players a way to opt out in settings.
A news site with ads uses a consent tool that applies the California rules by location.
A data broker must delete a person's data after a request through the state Delete Act platform.
Regulators check sites with test browsers that send an opt out signal, then see whether tags still fire.

risks: Fines for sites that ignore opt outs

technical_bounds: Applies to businesses above revenue or data thresholds
